title: Design, Build, Test, Repeat
short: Change one thing at a time, run several trials, and record the success rate honestly.
trouble: Students change three things at once and can't tell which one helped.

blocks.html: A robot that worked once is a good start. A robot that works 19 times out of 20 is a finished project. The difference is testing.
Engineers work in a cycle: design, build, test, change one thing, test again. Run each version several times, record every run in a test log, and compare success rates.

blocks.html: If you change three things at once and it gets better, you cannot tell which change helped, or whether one hurt. With only a few runs, luck can look like progress; more runs make the comparison fair. Competitions like FIRST reward teams that test this way.
Changing three things at once, or only writing down the runs that worked.

blocks.text: A project ladder for your portfolio

items: Rung 1: a line follower with two light sensors and a state machine.
Rung 2: an obstacle avoider with an ultrasonic sensor and encoder odometry; log its square-test drift.
Rung 3: a two-joint servo arm that reaches typed-in targets with inverse kinematics.
Rung 4: a wheel-speed PID controller with a plot of step responses at three gains.
Rung 5: a ball chaser with a camera and color thresholding.
Rung 6: the same robot in ROS 2: nodes for the camera, the controller and the motors, tested first in simulation.

blocks.html: For each rung, write a one-page report: the goal, a photo or short video, the code, the test log, and what you would change next. That stack of pages is a portfolio.
